name: Halcova Library — Foundations pack (starter)
description: Genre origins (T4), era snapshots (T3), and label/publisher lore (T5) with the highest hit-rate per entry. 31 entries across records and books — the working template for the Core 500 bank.

coverage.model: Foundations match any item in a matched genre/label/year band, so hit-rate per entry is high; per-artist T1/T2/T6/T7 packs close the remaining gap.
coverage.betaNote: Validate the ~50–70% item-coverage estimate on a typical mixed 40-item collection before international launch (lore-layer-plan.md §8).
coverage.factsToFlag: F-0018 (hip-hop origin party) and F-0020 (first heavy-metal band) ship only their uncontested cores with hedged [DISPUTED] framing; F-0027 (Latin American Boom) is flagged [CULT] for the es local-hero pack.

fact.text: The blues grew out of African-American work songs, spirituals, and field hollers in the Deep South in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. W.C. Handy's 'Memphis Blues' (1912) is among the first blues compositions to reach print and helped carry the blues to a national audience.
fact.voice: Before vinyl, the blues lived in the field and the church. Then W.C. Handy wrote one down — and it never went back.

fact.text: The phrase 'rock and roll' appears in blues records as early as the 1920s (e.g. 'My Man Rocks Me (With One Steady Roll)', 1922). Cleveland disc jockey Alan Freed is widely credited with popularizing the term for the new genre in the early 1950s.
fact.voice: The words are older than the genre — by the time Alan Freed put them on the radio, they'd been swinging around in blues lyrics for decades.

fact.text: Historians still argue over the 'first rock and roll record'. The most frequently named candidate is 'Rocket 88' (1951), credited to Jackie Brenston with Ike Turner's Kings of Rhythm, recorded at Sam Phillips' Memphis studio — but other sources make the case for earlier R&B tracks or Elvis Presley's 'That's All Right' (1954). The uncontested core: several early-1950s records share the claim.
fact.voice: Ask three historians which record started rock and roll and you'll get four answers. The crate doesn't care — it owns them all.

fact.text: Jazz developed in New Orleans in the early 20th century, blending blues, ragtime, brass-band, and Creole traditions. The first jazz recordings were made in 1917 by the Original Dixieland Jass Band ('Livery Stable Blues').

Blue Note Records was founded in 1939 in New York by Alfred Lion (with Max Margulis); photographer Francis Wolff joined in 1941. Lion and Wolff together shaped the label's signature hard-bop sound and its iconic covers.
fact.voice: Two Berlin-born friends, one tiny label, and the most photographed record sleeves in jazz.

fact.text: Motown Record Corporation was founded by Berry Gordy in Detroit in 1959; the name comes from 'Motor Town'. The Miracles' 'Shop Around' (1960) became one of Motown's first million-sellers.

Columbia introduced the 12-inch long-playing record (LP) in 1948; RCA Victor introduced the 45 rpm single in 1949. Those two formats defined the record store — and the crate — for the next five decades.
fact.voice: Two speeds, one destiny: the LP for the deep listen, the 45 for the hit. Your crate is just their reunion.

fact.text: The Sex Pistols' 'Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols' (released October 1977) was the band's only studio album and a cornerstone of the punk movement in the UK.
fact.voice: One album, one middle finger, one genre reshaped. The shelf has never been the same since.

title: Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols
label: Virgin

fact.text: Edgar Allan Poe's 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' (1841) is widely credited as the first modern detective story, introducing the analytical detective and the locked-room mystery.

title: The Murders in the Rue Morgue

fact.text: Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein' (1818) is frequently cited as one of the earliest works of science fiction, though scholars also credit later writers such as H.G. Wells. The label 'science fiction' itself was popularized by Hugo Gernsback in the 1920s.
fact.voice: A ghost-story contest in a rainy Swiss villa, an 18-year-old author, and arguably the first science-fiction novel. Some shelves are born legendary.

title: Frankenstein
The Time Machine
Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas

fact.text: Penguin Books was founded by Allen Lane in London in 1935. Its first ten sixpenny paperbacks — with the now-iconic orange covers — are credited with starting the paperback revolution and making good books affordable.
fact.voice: In 1935 a publisher decided a good book should cost the same as a packet of cigarettes. The paperback never looked back.

fact.text: Everyman's Library was founded in 1906 by publisher J.M. Dent in London, with the aim of making the classics affordable to 'everyman' — the motto that still names the imprint.
Johannes Gutenberg introduced movable-type printing in Europe in the mid-15th century. The Gutenberg Bible (c. 1455) is the earliest major book printed with movable type; around 180 copies were made.
fact.voice: Before Gutenberg, a library was a luxury for kings. After him, it became something you could fill — and your shelf is the proof.

fact.text: Astérix, by writer René Goscinny and artist Albert Uderzo, first appeared in October 1959 in the first issue of the French comics magazine Pilote. It is one of the best-selling comic series in the world.
fact.voice: Le petit Gaulois arrived in 1959 with a magic potion and a healthy disrespect for Rome — and French shelves never looked back.

fact.text: Will Eisner's 'A Contract with God' (1978) is widely credited with popularizing the term 'graphic novel' in the English-speaking world, though the term appears in print before that date and the 'first graphic novel' title is itself contested. The uncontested core: Eisner's book reframed how comics could be sold and shelved.
fact.voice: A 60-something cartoonist decided a comic could be a novel. Bookshops have been rearranging their shelves ever since.

fact.text: Rhythm and blues grew out of blues, gospel, and jazz in the 1940s. The term was coined in the late 1940s by Billboard writer Jerry Wexler — later a producer at Atlantic Records — to replace 'race music.' Soul music then emerged in the 1950s and 1960s as R&B fused with gospel, with its roots in the Black church.
fact.voice: A name a music journalist coined because 'race music' wouldn't do — and a whole crate of records that owe him one.

fact.text: Modern country music traces to the Bristol Sessions of 1927, when Victor producer Ralph Peer recorded the Carter Family and Jimmie Rodgers in Bristol, on the Tennessee–Virginia border. The sessions are often called the 'big bang' of country music.
fact.voice: One town, two weeks, and the recording sessions people still call country music's big bang.

fact.text: Hip hop emerged in the Bronx, New York, in the early 1970s at neighborhood block parties. DJ Kool Herc's party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in 1973, where he extended the instrumental breaks of funk and soul records, is widely cited as a foundational moment — though the culture grew across the decade through DJing, MCing, breaking, and graffiti.
fact.voice: Two turntables, a longer break, and a culture that was built on a Bronx street corner.

fact.text: Reggae developed in Jamaica in the late 1960s, growing out of ska and rocksteady with a slower tempo and the offbeat 'one drop' rhythm. Bob Marley and the Wailers carried the music to a global audience in the 1970s.
fact.voice: From Kingston sound systems to beaches on the other side of the world — the beat that refused to stay home.

fact.text: Heavy metal emerged in the late 1960s and early 1970s, largely in Birmingham, England, where bands including Black Sabbath, Led Zeppelin, and Deep Purple turned up the volume and distortion. Which band truly 'started' the genre is contested; the uncontested core is that these bands, among others, defined its sound.
fact.voice: A city of factories, three bands with very loud guitars, and an argument that still won't die. The crate just turns it up.

fact.text: Atlantic Records was founded in New York in 1947 by Ahmet Ertegun and Herb Abramson. It became home to landmark R&B and soul — Ray Charles, Aretha Franklin, Otis Redding — and later to rock bands including Led Zeppelin.
fact.voice: A label that bet on soul before the charts did — and that your crate keeps paying back.

fact.text: Chess Records was founded in Chicago in 1950 by brothers Phil and Leonard Chess. It became a cornerstone of electric Chicago blues — Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf — and of early rock and roll with Chuck Berry and Bo Diddley.
fact.voice: Two brothers, a South Side storefront, and some of the loudest, most important blues ever put on wax.

fact.text: Disco rose through the 1970s from dance clubs rooted in Black, Latino, and gay club culture, and peaked with the 1977 film 'Saturday Night Fever' and its Bee Gees soundtrack, which helped make the genre a global phenomenon.
fact.voice: Four-on-the-floor, a mirrorball, and a soundtrack that still fills dance floors — and crates.

fact.text: The Beatles' February 1964 appearance on 'The Ed Sullivan Show' in the US opened the British Invasion — a wave of UK acts, including the Rolling Stones, the Kinks, and the Who, that dominated American charts through the mid-1960s.
fact.voice: One Sunday night on American television, and suddenly the record stores stocked British accents.

fact.text: Horace Walpole's 'The Castle of Otranto' (1764) is widely credited as the first Gothic novel. Its second edition carried the subtitle 'A Gothic Story,' and its ruined castles, supernatural events, and melodrama came to define the genre.
fact.voice: Ruined castles, creaking doors, and a genre that's been giving shelves nightmares since 1764.

fact.text: J.R.R. Tolkien's 'The Hobbit' (1937) and 'The Lord of the Rings' (1954–55) are widely credited with establishing modern fantasy as a distinct genre, shaping the secondary worlds, invented languages, and epic quests that followed.
fact.voice: An Oxford professor built a whole world out of languages and maps — and every fantasy shelf since is walking in his footsteps.

fact.text: The Latin American 'Boom' of the 1960s and 1970s brought a surge of internationally celebrated novelists — Gabriel García Márquez, Mario Vargas Llosa, Julio Cortázar, Carlos Fuentes — often associated with magical realism and experimental narrative.
fact.voice: A continent's stories, one decade, and two Nobel laureates later — your shelf still isn't done with them.

fact.text: Faber and Faber was founded in 1929 by Geoffrey Faber, growing out of the earlier firm Faber & Gwyer. T.S. Eliot joined as an editor in 1925 and became a director, publishing his own poetry with the house, which became one of the most influential literary imprints of the 20th century.
fact.voice: A publisher with a poet at the editor's desk — the 20th century's literature kept walking in after him.

fact.text: Anchor Books was launched in 1953 by Jason Epstein at Doubleday. It is widely credited with pioneering the American trade paperback — serious books in affordable, bookstore-friendly paper editions.
fact.voice: Before 1953, paperbacks were cheap thrillers. Jason Epstein made them the library you could actually afford.

fact.text: The Beat Generation was a 1950s American literary movement centered in New York and San Francisco, known for spontaneous, experimental prose and poetry — most famously Allen Ginsberg's 'Howl' (1956) and Jack Kerouac's 'On the Road' (1957).
fact.voice: Typewriters, road trips, and a refusal to sit still — the beats turned restlessness into literature.

fact.text: In the mid-19th century, many novels first appeared in serial form, published a chapter or two at a time in magazines or part issues. Charles Dickens's 'The Pickwick Papers' (1836–37) helped make serial publication hugely popular, and his later novels were eagerly awaited installment by installment.
fact.voice: Before binge-watching, there was serial reading: a month of waiting between chapters, and readers loved every second.
